solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Flight whose path circles before a landing

definitions.text: Flight whose path circles before a landing

parts.words: Flight whose path circles before a landing
parts.note: surface reading: an aircraft flying a holding pattern before it touches down

parts.words: Flight whose path circles before a landing
parts.note: setter's reading: a flight of steps that winds round and round up to the next floor's landing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flight' and 'landing' both have aviation and staircase senses; the circling path belongs to the stairs, not a plane.
explanation.definitionFit: A flight of steps that coils round a central column on its way to a landing is exactly this kind of staircase.

clue.text: Country pest found under base of trees

indicators.note: in a down entry, being under something means being written after it
in a down clue the base of a word is its bottom, that is its final letter

parts.note: the bottom letter of trees
a pest is a pain, a nuisance

explanation.surface: An insect pest lurking beneath the roots of trees somewhere in a country.
explanation.definitionFit: Spain is a European nation, so it is an instance of a country.

clue.text: Where MCC member might be expecting a delivery?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: literally inside the club, where a member of the Marylebone Cricket Club would be found
second meaning: British slang for pregnant, awaiting the delivery of a baby

explanation.walkthrough: The MCC is the Marylebone Cricket Club, based at Lord's; the cricket setting makes a delivery look like a bowled ball, but it is a birth.
explanation.definitionFit: A club member is literally inside the club, and the idiom means expecting a child, so both senses fit.

clue.text: A course of action on vacation

parts.note: taken as written
a way is a method or course of action

explanation.surface: Someone choosing a plan for what to do while on holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on vacation is not at home but off on holiday, which is the adverb's sense.

clue.text: Quiet times full of pressure for climbing people

parts.note: sh is the call for quiet

indicators.note: something full of a thing holds it inside, so one piece wraps round another

parts.note: eras are periods of time
P is the physics symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: Calm periods under strain for mountaineers on an ascent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climbing' suggests a down-clue reversal, but here it describes the people being defined.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherpas are a Himalayan people famous as mountain guides and porters, so a people known for climbing.

clue.text: Province: one close to Victoria, Australia originally

parts.note: Prince Albert was Queen Victoria's husband, as close to her as anyone

indicators.note: originally points to how a word begins, so only its opening letter is used

parts.note: the opening letter of Australia

explanation.surface: A province near Victoria in Australia, pointing the solver at the Australian state.
explanation.walkthrough: Victoria looks like the Australian state, but it is the Queen; her consort gives the first part.
explanation.definitionFit: Alberta is one of Canada's provinces, named after a daughter of Victoria and Albert.

clue.text: Stones cover cut by Love is unlikely to fail

indicators.note: a word cut by another is split open with that other placed in the gap

parts.note: rocks are stones
love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O
a lid is a cover

explanation.surface: A stone-built cover strengthened by love is a dependable thing.
explanation.walkthrough: Stones and cover are side by side, and Love slots between them; the clue lists cover first but the letter O cuts in after ROCKS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rock-solid is utterly dependable and firm, so it is unlikely to fail.

clue.text: Worship a party communist (mostly)

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
a do is a party
red is a common name for a communist

explanation.surface: A godless communist party wrongly said to worship something.
explanation.definitionFit: To adore is to love deeply and revere, a close synonym of the verb worship.

clue.text: Limit for data brought in by new internet host

indicators.note: a thing brought in by another goes inside it
making something new remakes it, so these letters come out in a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: a limit is an edge, here the closing edge, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of data

explanation.surface: A cap on data usage introduced by a fresh internet hosting company.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters of internet take in the last letter of data near their end. 'Host' looks like a web server, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To entertain guests is to receive and look after them, the verb sense of host.

clue.text: Start off champion about gold upset in race

indicators.note: one piece placed in another sits inside it

parts.note: an ace is a champion, a top performer

indicators.note: upset means tipped over, so the word for gold is turned round
about means around, so the champion word goes round the rest

parts.note: the TT, the Tourist Trophy, is the Isle of Man motorcycle race
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: A star rider sets off after gold in a race goes badly for them.
explanation.walkthrough: The containers nest: the turned gold goes into the race first, and that pair then sits inside the champion.
explanation.definitionFit: To actuate a machine is to set it going, so it means to start something off.

clue.text: Help! rented already? Get Cold Feet?

parts.note: to back someone is to help or support them
a video or library book already rented is out

explanation.surface: Someone panicking that a place they wanted is already let, and losing their nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals on Cold Feet nod to the British TV sitcom of that name; they are there only to mislead.
explanation.definitionFit: To back out is to withdraw from a commitment through nerves, which is the idiom of getting cold feet.

clue.text: Those against lad reversing over European

indicators.note: reversing means going backwards, so the word for lad is read right to left

parts.note: a son is a lad, a boy
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: Opponents of a young man reversing his car over a European.
explanation.definitionFit: In a vote, the noes are the people voting against, as in 'the noes have it'.

clue.text: Stores wrap up gear for game types

indicators.note: to wrap up here is read as a word that is folded and bundled, its letters jumbled

parts.note: both words taken as fodder

explanation.surface: Shops bundle up kit for sporty people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrap' does double duty in the surface but only its letters count; 'up' signals the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Sportswear is clothing for athletes, so it is the kit worn by people who play games.

clue.text: High-flyer that's head of satellite channels

parts.note: a gull is a seabird, flying high
i.e. abbreviates id est, 'that is'

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of satellite

explanation.surface: An ambitious person who runs the satellite television channels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High-flyer' and 'channels' both suggest broadcasting executives, but the flyer is a bird and the channels are carved by water.
explanation.definitionFit: Gullies are narrow ravines or gutters that carry water, so they are channels.

clue.text: One dressing as herring must get changed

indicators.note: something that must get changed is altered, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: both words taken as fodder

explanation.surface: Someone getting dressed up as a herring for a fancy-dress party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dressing' suggests putting on clothes, but it is dressing a plate of food.
explanation.definitionFit: A garnisher decorates food with garnish, which is what a cook does when dressing a dish.

clue.text: Stupid to take in old lady using native tongue

indicators.note: to take in is to receive inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: idiotic means stupid
one's old lady is one's mother, ma

explanation.surface: A foolish rebuke for bringing your mother along while speaking your mother tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatic language is natural to a native speaker, using the expressions of their own tongue.

clue.text: City finally to dump squad leader for northern ace

indicators.note: to dump one letter for another is to throw it out and put the other in its place

parts.note: at last means finally

indicators.note: 'leader' keeps only the first letter of 'squad'

parts.note: the leading letter of squad, the one dumped
N is the abbreviation for northern
A is short for ace, as on playing cards

explanation.surface: A city at last dropping its team captain in favour of a star player from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: In AT LAST the S is swapped for N, and A is then added.
explanation.definitionFit: Atlanta is the capital city of the US state of Georgia.

clue.text: Second person supporting lead anaesthetist?

parts.note: surface reading: a deputy, the second-in-command backing the leader
setter's reading: an anaesthetist numbs patients, so is jokingly a 'numb-er', and his assistant would be the second such one

explanation.walkthrough: The joke reads the first word of the phrase as 'numb-er', one who numbs, rather than as a count.
explanation.definitionFit: A deputy or right-hand man is called the number two, and the pun makes a numbing assistant the second numb-er.

clue.text: Pants chafe and slip

parts.note: to chafe is to rub
a bish is British slang for a mistake or slip

explanation.surface: Underwear that rubs and slides about uncomfortably.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like underwear; in British slang it means worthless nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling something pants in British slang means it is rubbish, of poor quality.

clue.text: Little drink by dock to get thus?

definitions.text: Little drink by dock to get thus?

parts.note: a half is a half-pint of beer, a small drink
to dock is to cut, as in docking wages

explanation.surface: Having a quick drink by the docks to end up in this state.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: one way to get drunk is drinking by the dock. Half-cut is British slang for tipsy.
explanation.definitionFit: Half-cut is informal British for drunk, the state you reach after drinking by the quayside.

clue.text: Site of corporation sign by black-centred poster?

indicators.note: centred with something means having it placed in the middle

parts.note: an ad, an advertisement, is a poster
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
an omen is a sign

explanation.surface: A company logo beside a dark poster, as if describing an advertising site.
explanation.walkthrough: Corporation is a dated British joke word for a large pot belly, so its site is the belly.
explanation.definitionFit: A corporation in this sense is a paunch, and a paunch is located on the belly.

clue.text: Island colonist, one with 18 guards

indicators.note: the answer to 18 means chopped in two, so only the front part of the next word is used

parts.note: ants live in colonies
Roman numeral one
taken as written, before trimming

explanation.surface: An island settler, a single person accompanied by a group of guards.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 down is HALF-CUT, used here literally: guards cut in half leaves its first three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Antigua is a Caribbean island, part of the nation of Antigua and Barbuda.

clue.text: Unfinished poem client wants rewriting

indicators.note: rewriting means the text is put down again in a different form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: both words taken as fodder

explanation.surface: A customer wants a half-written verse redone.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unfinished lacks parts still to be done, so it is incomplete, a straight synonym.

clue.text: Grunt carrying my or the Queen's best friend?

indicators.note: in a down entry, a piece carrying another holds it up on top, so that other comes first

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'
a grunt is slang for a US infantryman, a GI

explanation.surface: A soldier with a fond question about who is the monarch's closest companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks like a possessive but is the exclamation, which COR also is.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen Elizabeth II famously kept corgis, so the dog breed is jokingly her best friend.

clue.text: Hot and, out of head, cry "I'm in trouble!"

indicators.note: being out of its head means the word has lost its first letter

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps
a yelp is a sharp cry

explanation.surface: Feverish and delirious, someone calls out that they are in difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: Help! is the exclamation of someone in distress, the same cry as 'I'm in trouble!'

clue.text: Second gin brought up for constituents

indicators.note: in a down entry, brought up means raised from bottom to top, so read backwards

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a gin is a snare or trap

explanation.surface: A second glass of gin served to voters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gin' looks like the drink, but it is an animal trap.
explanation.definitionFit: Constituents are the component parts of a whole, so parts is a straight synonym.

clue.text: Tough slice of rump dons ate

indicators.note: to don is to put on, so one word wears the other inside it

parts.note: to have a meal is to eat, so had means ate

indicators.note: a slice is only a small piece, here the opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of rump

explanation.surface: University dons ate a chewy cut of rump steak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' looks like the academics, but it is the verb meaning puts on.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard and tough are synonyms, describing something firm or difficult, like overcooked meat.

clue.text: Free-thinker rejected quote about hospital

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the whole string that follows runs backwards

parts.note: to cite is to quote
re means about, concerning
H is the map abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: An independent thinker whose words about a hospital were thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a container signal, but here it is RE, joined to the other pieces before everything is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A heretic holds opinions against official doctrine, so is a free-thinker.

clue.text: Hard worker good with roofing support

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
a rafter is a beam supporting a roof

explanation.surface: A diligent builder good at putting up roof timbers.
explanation.walkthrough: Graft is British slang for hard work, so a grafter is a hard worker.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a grafter is someone who works hard, from graft meaning toil.

clue.text: Come down heavily on addict new grass set off

indicators.note: set off as in exploded, so the letters are blown apart and land in a new order

parts.note: the words as printed, but the parse needs an A they do not supply: the setter's slip
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A drug user cracks down hard after some fresh cannabis kicks in.
explanation.walkthrough: As published online the letters are one A short, a setter's slip; the print edition, 'on an addict grass', supplies it. N joins the jumbled letters. Grass is slang for cannabis.
explanation.definitionFit: To rain cats and dogs is an idiom for raining very heavily, so to pour down.
